title: Charge
subtitle: Design a clear commitment, a reachable escape, and a useful recovery.
summary: The boss aims, locks its direction, and charges forward. It cannot turn after the lock.
overview: Charge is a high-speed attack: the boss aims, locks its direction, and rushes forward without turning. The mechanic works well when the clear lock makes the path predictable, sideways movement provides a reachable response, and recovery creates an opening for a counterattack.

combatFeel.title: How a charge can feel
combatFeel.intro: These are possible design intentions, not fixed traits of every charge. The diagram demonstrates one locked-direction charge; the variants below describe other ways to tune that same rule.

variants.label: Relentless
variants.tuning: Keep the lock cue brief but distinct, then repeat charges with shorter gaps. The boss can feel aggressive without removing the time for ordinary sideways clearance or a useful counterattack after each pass.

connection.body: The spacing between attacks creates sustained pressure; test the sequence as well as each charge.

variants.label: Weighty
variants.tuning: Hold the aiming pose longer, emphasize acceleration and impact, then give the boss a longer recovery. One charge can feel imposing while its direction remains fixed and its escape route stays readable.

connection.body: Preparation builds the expectation of force; a distinct release cue marks when danger begins.

learning: Tune tracking, the lock cue, the danger lane, and recovery.

demo.title: Test the attack
phaseDescriptions: The boss prepares the charge and tracks the player's position.
Direction locks and the player clears the lane with ordinary sideways movement.
The boss crosses the arena on the locked path; the next charge begins from the other side.
demo.reducedMotion: Autoplay is disabled by the reduced-motion setting. Use the timeline slider to inspect the loop.
demo.gamePlaying: Dodge the locked charge, then move close to the boss during recovery to strike automatically.
demo.diagramDescription: A looping charge diagram. The boss alternates attacks from above and below while the player always moves sideways out of the lane.

steps.title: When does tracking stop?
steps.body: Choose a fixed moment. Mark it with a pose, sound, or effect.

steps.title: Can the lane be cleared?
steps.body: Compare lane width, player speed, and the time between lock and impact.

steps.title: Is recovery useful?
steps.body: Include the time needed to return to range and complete an attack.

mistakes.title: Unclear lock
mistakes.body: If tracking and lock look the same, hits feel arbitrary.

mistakes.title: Fake opening
mistakes.body: If recovery ends before the player can reach the boss, the promised opening is not real.

designNotes.title: Start with normal movement
designNotes.body: Make the basic escape work without a special ability unless that ability is the lesson.

designNotes.title: Match collision and visuals
designNotes.body: The visible danger lane must match the real hitbox.

designNotes.title: Retest after upgrades
designNotes.body: Movement, range, damage, and invulnerability can change how the attack works.

story.title: Use a clear arena
story.body: A long, open lane makes the attack easy to read. Avoid obstacles that hide the boss or the escape route.

adaptation.title: Respect player upgrades
adaptation.body: Test the attack against the abilities already available to the player. If the boss blocks an attack, show it clearly and keep another response useful.

distinction.title: Charge ≠ dash ≠ lunge
distinction.body: A charge threatens a full lane. A dash changes position. A lunge is a short attack. This page shows one kind of charge.

lensNotes.body: A pose, sound, or effect announces both the charge and the exact moment tracking stops. The cue and the rule must agree.
After lock, the boss gives up steering in exchange for speed and reach. This commitment makes prediction possible.
The attack creates a lane, not a point. Test its width against the player's full collision shape, arena space, and camera.
At least one response must be reachable with the movement the player already owns. Extra skills may add options without becoming silently required.
A stronger, longer charge earns a clearer tell and a useful recovery window. Threat and opportunity are tuned together.
The boss tests movement and cue-reading taught before the encounter. Upgrades should change the solution space without erasing the mechanic.

examples.body: A short tell leads into a straight charge that stops at terrain. Obstacles and lane width define the attack.
Its second phase chains fast charges from different angles. Shorter gaps turn one readable move into sustained pressure.
A brief lean-back signals a horizontal dash. The small arena and high damage demand a very clear cue.
Long runs, wide turns, and walls make momentum part of the encounter. The charge stays readable even when its path curves.
The lowered head announces a long rush. Body size and the open arena make distance and lateral clearance easy to read.
Brief tracking leads into a long arena-crossing charge. A circular room and 3D camera make the safe side harder to judge.
